lesson.title: Between the Curves: Using Integrals to Measure Area
lesson.summary: When two curves cross, the area trapped between them can be found by integrating the difference of the two functions between their intersection points, turning a single-curve tool into one that measures the space bounded by two functions at once.
lesson.body:
A single definite integral finds the area between one curve and the x-axis, but many practical problems ask for the area trapped between two curves instead, such as the space between a supply curve and a demand curve, or between two paths traced over time. The idea extends naturally: if one function, call it the top function, stays above another, the bottom function, across some interval, then the area between them is found by integrating the difference, top minus bottom, across that interval. Subtracting first makes sense because at every single x-value, the vertical gap between the two curves is exactly (top function value) minus (bottom function value), and the integral simply adds up all of those infinitely thin vertical gaps across the interval.

The first step in almost every area-between-curves problem is finding where the two curves intersect, since those intersection points become the limits of integration, marking where one function stops being on top and the boundary of the trapped region begins and ends. Intersection points are found the same way as always: set the two functions equal to each other and solve.

Here is a fully worked example. Find the area of the region enclosed between y = x² and y = x + 2. First find the intersection points by setting the functions equal: x² = x + 2, which rearranges to x² - x - 2 = 0. Factoring gives (x - 2)(x + 1) = 0, so x = 2 or x = -1. Testing a value between them, say x = 0, shows that x + 2 = 2 is larger than x² = 0 there, so the line y = x + 2 is the top function and the parabola y = x² is the bottom function across this interval. The area is ∫ from -1 to 2 of [(x + 2) - x²] dx.

Finding the antiderivative of (x + 2) - x² gives F(x) = x²/2 + 2x - x³/3. Evaluate at the top limit, x = 2: F(2) = (2)²/2 + 2(2) - (2)³/3 = 4/2 + 4 - 8/3 = 2 + 4 - 8/3 = 6 - 8/3 = 18/3 - 8/3 = 10/3. Evaluate at the bottom limit, x = -1: F(-1) = (-1)²/2 + 2(-1) - (-1)³/3 = 1/2 - 2 - (-1/3) = 1/2 - 2 + 1/3. Using a common denominator of 6: 3/6 - 12/6 + 2/6 = -7/6. Subtracting, F(2) - F(-1) = 10/3 - (-7/6) = 10/3 + 7/6. Converting 10/3 to sixths gives 20/6, so 20/6 + 7/6 = 27/6 = 4.5. The enclosed area is exactly 4.5 square units. Since both curves meet at x = -1 and x = 2, the gap between them naturally shrinks to zero at both endpoints and grows to its widest in between, and the integral captures that entire changing gap in one calculation rather than requiring separate area formulas for each little piece of the region.
